claims.text: As-deposited HEA coatings can contain an ultra-fine near-surface nanocrystalline or partially amorphous layer.
The near-surface ultra-fine layer is the primary agent governing enhanced wear resistance.
The ultra-fine layer increases adaptive surface hardness.
As-deposited HEA coatings typically have multicomponent microstructures that can include nanocrystalline or amorphous-like regions and complex phase distributions.
Pre-deformation can controllably induce and vary the thickness or extent of a near-surface nanocrystalline or partially amorphous layer.
Thermal annealing can controllably induce and vary the thickness or extent of a near-surface nanocrystalline or partially amorphous layer.
Microstructural evolution is active during sliding or abrasion at moderate loads, speeds, and ambient temperatures.
The induced ultra-fine layer enhances local hardness.
The induced ultra-fine layer promotes adaptive surface strengthening during wear.
The induced ultra-fine layer impedes crack propagation.
The modified near-surface microstructure dynamically accommodates shear stresses.
A thicker induced ultra-fine near-surface layer will produce a lower friction coefficient than the as-deposited baseline.
A thicker induced ultra-fine near-surface layer will produce a lower wear rate than the as-deposited baseline.
The predicted reduction in wear rate results from enhanced surface hardness and reduced microcrack formation.
The proposed relationship should hold under moderate wear conditions typical of protective coatings.
At extreme loads, speeds, or temperatures, other failure mechanisms may dominate and disrupt the predicted relationship.

contradictions.description: The layer is described as forming in the as-deposited state, but the treatment is also described as inducing that layer, while the baseline is only defined as lacking controlled treatment rather than lacking the layer. Thus, the intended mediator contrast between treated and baseline samples is internally ambiguous.
